deep.reconstruction:
The page holds two complete tables of biquadratic (quartic) residue classes. The neighbouring pages give the same kind of table for p=293, 281, 233 and 229.

Header data for each prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4):
- p = a^2 + b^2 with a odd and b even.
- f is a square root of -1 mod p, normalised by a + b f ≡ 0 (mod p), equivalently a f ≡ b.
- g is a primitive root.

Class definitions. Following the Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum (TRB I, 1828), a nonzero residue x falls in:
- A if x^((p-1)/4) ≡ 1,
- B if it is ≡ f,
- C if it is ≡ -1,
- D if it is ≡ -f.
The lists were evidently produced as index classes: x = g^k sorted by k mod 4. This agrees with the criterion only if g^((p-1)/4) ≡ f. That explains the correction of g from 11 to 5 for p=277 (my inference): 11 lies in D, i.e. 11^69 ≡ -f, whereas 5^69 ≡ 217 = f.

(1) p = 277:
- 277 = 9^2 + 14^2 and (p-1)/4 = 69.
- f = 217: 217^2 = 47089 = 170·277 - 1, so 217^2 ≡ -1.
- Normalisation: 9 + 14·217 = 3047 = 11·277, so a + b f ≡ 0.
- g = 5. Repeated squaring gives 5^4 ≡ 71, 5^8 ≡ 55, 5^16 ≡ -22, 5^32 ≡ -70, 5^64 ≡ 191. Hence 5^69 ≡ 191·71·5 ≡ 217 = f, so 5 ∈ B. Also 5^138 ≡ -1.
- Class sizes: A, B, C, D each list 69 numbers, 276 in total.
- Since p ≡ 5 (mod 8), -1 ∈ C. Therefore C = -A and D = -B. I verified both relations entry by entry and they hold exactly.
- f = 217 ∈ B and 2 ∈ D. This matches Gauss's theorem for p ≡ 5 (mod 8) with this normalisation: 2 ∈ B if b ≡ 2 (mod 8), and 2 ∈ D if b ≡ 6 (mod 8); here b = 14.

(2) p = 269:
- 269 = 13^2 + 10^2 and (p-1)/4 = 67.
- f = 187: 187^2 = 34969 = 130·269 - 1, so 187^2 ≡ -1.
- Normalisation: 13·187 = 2431 ≡ 10 = b.
- g = 2. Repeated squaring gives 2^8 ≡ -13, 2^16 ≡ 169, 2^32 ≡ 47, 2^64 ≡ 57. Hence 2^67 ≡ 456 ≡ 187 = f, so 2 ∈ B. Here b = 10 ≡ 2 (mod 8), consistent with the theorem above.
- f itself lies in D, since f^67 = f^3 = -f.
- B and D have 67 entries each. A and C have only 66 each (see errors).
- C = -A, and D = -B as far as checked.
- A is cyclic of prime order 67, generated by 5. Running through the powers of 5 reproduces every listed A entry except 119 (5^k ≡ 239 → 1195 ≡ 119 → 595 ≡ 57).

Purpose. The tables are raw material for the next page. There Gauss sorts the primes p by the class of a fixed small prime q = -23, -19, +17, +13 mod p, and records b/a mod q for each p. Two examples:
- For p = 277: 17 ∈ D, and b/a = 14/9 ≡ 11 (mod 17).
- For p = 269: 17 ∈ B, and b/a = 10/13 ≡ 6 (mod 17).
The page is thus empirical groundwork for determining the quartic character of q in terms of a, b mod q, i.e. biquadratic reciprocity.
errors: p=269, class A: the biquadratic residue 119 is missing. 5 generates A (order 67, prime), and 5^k runs ...239, 119, 57...; 119 appears in no class. The A list jumps 118 → 120 in the image too.
p=269, class C: correspondingly 150 = 269 - 119 is missing, since 150^67 ≡ -1. C jumps 149 → 151, so A and C have 66 entries instead of 67.
Not an error: for p=277 the primitive root was first written as 11, then struck out and replaced by g=5. 11 lies in class D (11^69 ≡ -f), so it would not give g^((p-1)/4) ≡ f.
No other discrepancies found. For p=277 all four classes have 69 entries, and C = -A, D = -B hold entry by entry.

results.what: Complete tables of quartic residue classes A, B, C, D (x^((p-1)/4) ≡ 1, f, -1, -f) for p=277 and p=269, with p = a^2 + b^2 and f normalised by a + b f ≡ 0
results.modern_name: quartic (biquadratic) residue character / quartic residue symbol tables

results.what: Class of 2 consistent with Gauss's criterion: for p ≡ 5 mod 8, 2 ∈ B if b ≡ 2 mod 8 and 2 ∈ D if b ≡ 6 mod 8 (277: b=14 gives D; 269: b=10 gives B)
Data feeding the next page's sorting of p by the class of q = 13, 17, -19, -23 against b/a mod q
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (stated in TRB II, 1832); proofs by Jacobi/Eisenstein (1844)

deep.surprise_reason: These are routine computational tables of the kind Gauss is known to have made for the Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum. They confirm his class conventions but contain no new result.

checkable.asserts: f=217 is a square root of -1 mod 277
g=5 lies in class B, i.e. g^((p-1)/4) ≡ f
the crossed-out g=11 lies in class D
17 ∈ D and 13 ∈ C mod 277, matching the next page's tables
p=269 data: a=13, b=10, f=187 with f^2 ≡ -1 and a f ≡ b
g=2 lies in class B mod 269
119 (class A) and 150 (class C) mod 269 are the residues omitted from the lists
class A for p=277 is exactly the set of biquadratic residues

transcription_corrections: No substantive corrections; the machine transcription agrees with the image. In p=277 class B, the '234' that looks like '2З4' in the image is 234. The p=269 class A list genuinely lacks 119 (118 → 120) and class C lacks 150 (149 → 151) in the manuscript itself.
Header for p=277: g was first written as 11 and struck out, with g = 5 added above. The struck value 11 is consistent with the image.
